## Slice 80 — the plugin-facing cross-owner request surface (§28.2's default nonblocking API) + the End dimension's missing region drain

- **The public interface (`api concurrent.CrossOwner`)**: the
  `CrossOwnerRouter`'s plugin-facing face over **`Server.crossOwner()`**
  — `submit(world, position, operation, action)` (the one-way command,
  §10.1's default), `submit(..., Supplier, BiConsumer)` (the
  result-carrying form), and the `deadlineTick` overload (the last tick
  the request may still apply). The `Request` handle: `state()`
  (QUEUED/APPLIED/FAILED/CANCELLED/EXPIRED/REFUSED), `cancel()` while
  queued, `resultNow()` (the non-blocking peek), `failure()`; the §28.9
  counters (submitted/refused/applied/failed/cancelled/expired).
- **The contract (§28.2's own rules, now enforced by an adapter)**:
  submission never blocks from any thread; the action AND the completion
  run in the TARGET owner's validated context at a tick boundary (the
  explicit completion context — never an arbitrary owner); admission is
  exactly-once per request (a fresh operation id each — a retry is a new
  request by contract); the per-target pending bound refuses LOUDLY (the
  handle reports REFUSED); a throwing action completes FAILED with the
  throwable and never kills the drain; cancellation skips without
  running; the deadline expires past its tick without running; at
  shutdown the queued requests flip CANCELLED with no completion
  (§28.5's invalidated-not-delivered law).
- **The engine view (`server/concurrent/CrossOwnerView`)**: the routing
  resolves the target position's region domain (the partitioned world's
  own lane — the same domain the tick-head boundary walk drains) or the
  unpartitioned world's own domain; the guard wraps every action (the
  cancel gate, the deadline gate against the target world's own tick
  clock at drain time, the failure isolation — the guard NEVER throws,
  so the router's counters stay its own "drained-without-throwing"
  telemetry and the view's counters carry the semantic outcomes); the
  live-handle registry keeps the shutdown walk bounded.
- **THE END'S MISSING REGION DRAIN (the engine fix)**: the tick head
  drained the overworld's and the nether's region intents but never the
  End's — an intent toward the End's region domain sat queued forever
  (the Slice 61 dimension landed after the drain wiring; nobody added
  its line). `endWorld.drainRegionIntents(crossOwnerRouter)` now rides
  the tick head beside its siblings.
- **The End's public presence (§27's surface fix)**: `Server.worlds()`
  grew the End (the collection stopped hiding the third dimension —
  EventApiAcceptanceTest's size assertion updated with it) and
  `EngineServer.endWorld()` joined `world()`/`netherWorld()`.
- Tests: `CrossOwnerApiAcceptanceTest` (9 — the target-context apply
  with the completion contract + the mutation landing, the failure
  isolation + the survivor, the cancel gate, the expiry gate + the
  on-own-tick apply, the loud backpressure with the REFUSED handle, the
  unpartitioned routing through the world's own domain, the live-engine
  foreign-thread apply through the public accessor, the End's drain
  through the live engine). The concurrent family + RegionBoundaryTest +
  Event/World/BlockEntity API acceptance green.

## Slice 81 — the piston + fluid observe hooks (§27.7's interaction-events wave) + THE FLUID FLOW FIX

- **THE ENGINE BUG THE WAVE FOUND (the slice's own headline)**:
  `FluidSystem.handleTarget`'s air gate compared an `Identifier`
  against a `BlockType` — `existing.equals(world.airType())` — ALWAYS
  false (the types never equal), so every AIR cell read as solid
  ground and **water/lava NEVER flowed into air on the live engine**
  (the source sat still; no test ever asserted a live spread, so the
  §472 family shipped broken). The one-line fix:
  `existing.equals(world.airType().identifier())`. Found by the
  acceptance harness itself — the flow events never fired, the debug
  walk showed the gate returning "blocked" for air.
- **The public `PistonMoveEvent`** (§27.7's pre-commit gate): fires
  inside the movement's boundary scope after the block-event re-check
  gates, BEFORE any world write — cancelling prevents the whole
  movement (the piston keeps its state, nothing moves or breaks, no
  sound; the vanilla arming's base-state flip is documented — a
  cancelled retract leaves the HEAD in place, the observable). The
  payload carries the resolver's own prospective lists (a fresh pure
  resolution — the push chain + the break list on extend, the pull
  chain on a sticky retract) + the facing (the public `Direction`),
  extending/sticky flags, and the world name.
- **The public `FluidFlowEvent`** (§27.7's pre-commit gate): fires per
  prospective landing cell right before the flow commits — cancelling
  behaves as blocked ground (the fluid never enters; the walk's own
  rules continue around it — a cancelled down-pour lets the source
  spread sideways, exactly as solid ground below would). The payload:
  the from/to cells, the fluid identifier, and the landing level (8
  for the falling column, the decayed level sideways). The contact
  reactions stay the post-commit BlockChangedEvent's own domain.
- **The wiring**: `PistonSystem.setEventBus` (the gate at both arms of
  `doBlockEventBody`) + `FluidSystem.setEventBus` (the gate in
  `handleTarget`, which grew the `from` cell parameter); the
  EngineServer boot wires both beside the other §27.7 gates;
  `FluidSystem.World` grew `name()` (the FluidWorld adapter answers
  the overworld's own name).
- Tests: `PistonFluidEventAcceptanceTest` (5 — the cancelled extend
  leaving the piston retracted + the stone unmoved + the after-cycle,
  the extend observation carrying the resolver lists + the facing +
  the flags, the cancelled retract keeping the head + the pulled
  block, the cancelled down-pour behaving as blocked ground with the
  sideways spread, the flow observation carrying the fluid + its
  level 8 down-pour). The piston family + the precipitation suite
  green (the fluid fix's own neighbors).

## Slice 82 — the furnace + hopper observe hooks (§27.7's interaction-events wave, the ledger's named rows)

- **The public `FurnaceBurnEvent`** (the ignite gate): fires at the
  ignite decision — cold furnace, smeltable input waiting, one fuel
  unit about to be consumed. Cancel keeps the fuel AND the furnace
  cold (the next tick re-attempts; nothing is lost). The payload: the
  fuel stack + the burn value in ticks.
- **The public `FurnaceSmeltEvent`** (the cook gate): fires at the
  200-tick term — one input about to be consumed, the result about to
  land. Cancel keeps both; the cycle's progress is already spent (the
  reference's own reset happens before the commit — a cancelled smelt
  restarts the cook cycle, exactly like a cycle whose result stopped
  fitting). The payload: the input stack + the would-be result stack.
- **The public `HopperTransferEvent`** (the transfer gate): fires per
  prospective item move inside the transfer's boundary scope —
  PUSH (one item toward the faced container), PULL (one from the
  container above), SUCK (the item entities in the collection box) —
  with the counterpart position + the one-item payload. Cancel keeps
  THIS item; the walk's own rules continue (the next slot's item gets
  its own event; a fully-cancelled cycle arms no cooldown).
- **The wiring**: `FurnaceBlockEntity` grew the `Gates` consult points
  (the ignite + the smelt completion, both before any slot mutation)
  wired by the manager's adapter (the world name captured at the tick
  entry — the gates run on the same tick thread); `HopperSystem` fires
  its own gate (it holds the world) at the three arms, each BEFORE the
  slot/entity mutation.

  hopper passes through the collection band (the in-band suck still

  1:1, op-2): the objectives family (list / add with the display name /
  remove / setdisplay over all 19 slot names), the players family (list /
  set / add / remove / reset both shapes / enable with the trigger gate /
  test with the * bounds / operation with all nine operators incl. the
  >< swap), the teams family (list both shapes / add / remove / empty /
  join with the sender-self arm / leave / option), and the reference's own
  `*` wildcard walk (re-run per score owner, the multi-wildcard refusal).
  The option color arm does the reference's own decoration walk (the
  prefix becomes the color's chat code, the suffix the reset). THE BUGS
  the tests caught: the option gate + switch compared the lowercased name
  against mixed-case literals (the visibility options silently fell
  through to the usage gate — the reference's equalsIgnoreCase flattened).
- **THE PERSISTENCE** (`ScoreboardDataStore`, world/scoreboard.json — the
  reference's scoreboard.dat role): objectives (name/criterion/display/
  render), teams (every field + the members), the display slots, and every
  score cell; saved on the shutdown + /save walk, restored at boot before
  the first join can sync it. The dependency-free JSON walk (the OpStore
  convention); a corrupt file degrades to a fresh board.
- **THE QUIRK PRESERVED**: the 1.8 command splitter has NO quote handling
  (Brigadier is 1.13+) — a quoted display name keeps its quote marks,
  exactly like the reference's parseText LiteralText walk (tested).
- Tests: `ScoreboardCommandTest` (4 — the objectives family end-to-end
  incl. the quote quirk + the unknown-criterion gate, the players family
  with the read-only gate + the operation set incl. the swap + the trigger
  enable + the test bounds, the teams family with the color decoration +
  the visibility options + join/leave/empty, the persistence round trip
  through shutdown + reload incl. the display slot + the team color +
  the member index). The command/player families green.

## Slice 87 — the titles wave (the text model + the 0x45/0x47 wire + the target selector + /title + /tellraw + the header/footer API)

- **THE TEXT MODEL** (`server/text/`, Text/Style/Formatting 1:1 over the
  dependency-free JSON walk): the GSON tree semantics ported whole — the
  bare-literal short form, the style fields inlined in the reference's own
  order (addStyle before the type dispatch), the with-args flattening (a
  bare literal arg becomes its raw string), the empty-array null quirk
  (fromJson("[]") answers null), and the insertion-vanishing quirk
  (Style.isEmpty omits the insertion field — an insertion-only style
  serializes as the bare form and drops it). ScoreText's content consults
  the live main board through the installed-supplier seam;
  TranslatableText's translation machinery is client-side (the no-locale
  fallback answers the key itself).
- **THE WIRE**: Title 0x45 (TitlesS2CPacket's write walk — the varint enum
  ordinal, the JSON text on TITLE/SUBTITLE, the three i32s on TIMES, the
  empty CLEAR/RESET arms) + Player List Header/Footer 0x47
  (TabListS2CPacket's two-text walk) over ClientLink's six new title verbs
  + the header/footer verb + the raw-JSON chat verb (Chat 0x02 at a
  position byte — the reference's sendMessage(Component)); the conformance
  rows + Protocol18's constants. The vanilla server NEVER sends 0x47 (the
  reference wires only the client handler) — the verb exists for the
  native API surface.
- **THE SELECTOR** (`server/command/TargetSelector` 1:1): the whole
  p/a/e/r walk over the engine's universe seam — the positional short
  form, type/xp/gamemode/team/score_/name/rm-r/ry-rx/c with the
  reference's own quirks (the p/a type-ignored quirk, the !type
  matches-players quirk, the r shuffle, the p/a/e distance sort, the c==1
  self-bias, the wrapDegrees windows, the negative-d box extension). The
  engine install: the live players + the living mobs per the reference's
  dimension ids (-1/0/1), the main board for the score_/team predicates.
  The engine's mobs carry no public uuid (the score owner key rides the
  name) and no tracked pitch (rx reads 0) — ledgered.
- **THE COMMANDS** (op-2): /title (TitleCommand 1:1 — the five arms with
  the exact args gates, the case-insensitive type names with the TITLE
  default, the strict times ints, the joined-string JSON parse with the
  tellraw jsonException root-cause refusal) + /tellraw (TellRawCommand
  1:1 — updateForEntity resolves the component against the receiving
  player, the delivery as the raw-JSON system chat line);
  TextUtils.updateForEntity 1:1 (the score-owner selector walk, the
  selector components into the listText "a, b and c" join, the translate
  args recursion) + CommandParse (parsePlayer's
  selector/uuid/name/not-found ladder, parseString, the strict parseInt).
- **THE 0x47 API**: Server.setTabListHeaderFooter(headerJson, footerJson)
  — the stored pair broadcast to every PLAYING session, later joins get
  the pair at their own burst (joinTabListHeaderFooter, called beside
  joinWorldBorder in the adapter's join walk); null clears to the wire's
  null-text form.

## Slice 91 — the §27 window family's re-sync wave + the public open-window surface (p1-p3, the chest arms open)

- **p1 — THE OPEN-WINDOW RE-SYNC (the furnace's own diff path generalized)**:
  EngineServer grew the three per-tick view fans over the furnace idiom —
  tickChestViewers (the world chest, the session's private ender grid, the
  chest minecart's own chest resolved by the mount id), tickHopperViewers
  (the world hopper, the hopper minecart's hopper by the mount id),
  tickDispenserViewers (the dispenser/dropper) — fired in the tick walk
  after the enchanting fan. V18ProtocolServer subscribes the three;
  V18Connection carries the per-window serial diffs
  (chestSlotsSynced/hopperSlotsSynced/dispenserSlotsSynced, captured at
  open by the beacon idiom) and re-syncs the open viewer's Window Items
  only when the container's slotsSerial moved: a plugin's setSlot through
  the public container views, the hopper system's own transfer, any
  engine-side write — all bump the same serial. HopperBlockEntity grew its
  own slotsSerial (the chest's pattern — the BE had none). The
  furnace/brewing/beacon stay on their per-tick view fans (already covered,

## Slice M1+M2 — the physics-solver foundation (Wave M opens)

- **M1 — the geometry + the gather**: the new `server/physics` package.
  `Aabb` — the 1:1 port of the reference's `util/math/Box.java` in
  ABSOLUTE world coordinates: `expanded` (the swept-motion face law —
  a negative delta grows the min face, a positive the max), `grown`/
  `contract`/`moved`/`union`, `intersects` (the reference's own
  half-open convention — touching faces never intersect), and the
  clipping trio `intersectX/intersectY/intersectZ` (lines 104-162
  verbatim: the box clips the axis limit to its own face distance ONLY
  when the two boxes overlap on the other two axes — a fall that never
  reaches the floor passes untouched, a fall that would pass through
  clips to exactly the ceiling). `EntityCollisionWorld` — the
  block-read surface (blockAt + the chunkLoaded gate + the
  borderContains consult; the caller owns the dimension context, the
  reference's own Entity.world law). `EntityCollisions` — the 1:1 port
  of `World.getCollisions(Entity, Box)` lines 897-940's BLOCK side:
  the cell band `floor(minX)..floor(maxX+1)` with the Y band starting
  ONE cell below (the reference's own `k - 1` — the 1.5-tall families
  poke through their ceiling so the cell below the region still
  contributes), the chunk gate (an unloaded column contributes
  nothing), the border law (a cell outside the world border reads as
  STONE for a body INSIDE the border — the reference's own flag/flag1
  walk — and real for a body already outside), and per cell the
  block's own `addCollisions` through the SAME `CollisionShapes`
  table the point queries read (`cellBoxes` — the new public view;
  the connection families resolve their arms against the cell's own
  neighbour probe, so the swept-box model and the point model read
  ONE law), each box offset into world coordinates and added only
  when it intersects the swept region.
- **M2 — the move itself**: `EntityMoveSolver` — the 1:1 port of
  `Entity.move` lines 390-585, the BODY model the ledger deferred from
  the collision-shape slice. The `Body` (the feet-centre x/y/z + the
  width/height the shape derives from, the reference's `setPosition`
  line 246 law, with `setPositionFromShape` recovering the position
  from the moved shape exactly like line 586's own tail); the
  `MoveLaw` (the per-family fields distilled: stepHeight — 0.5 the
  walkers, 0.0 the item bodies and falling blocks, 1.0 the horses;
  the sneaking edge-guard gate; noClip; inCobweb); the `Result` (the
  clipped deltas + collidingHorizontally/Vertically + onGround — the
  downward clip only, exactly line 563 — + the velocity-zeroing
  signals: the X clip zeroes velocityX, the Z clip velocityZ, the
  vertical clip velocityY through the reference's own
  `beforeCollision` default, + the cobweb zero). THE WALK ITSELF:
  the cobweb drag (0.25/0.05/0.25), the sneaking edge-guard (the
  0.05 shaved walk that never leaves the support — X alone, then Z,
  then the pair, lines 409-446 verbatim), the gather over the shape
  expanded by the motion, the Y clip then X then Z (each box in walk
  order), and THE STEP-HEIGHT RETRY (lines 469-545 verbatim — the
  two-pass up-and-over walk at the full intended motion, the
  squared-distance comparison d20 vs d10, the descending second pass,
  the keep-only-if-better comparison against the clipped walk). Pure
  geometry: no entity state crosses in or out — the caller owns the
  velocities, the fall distance, and the family side effects, exactly
  the reference's own Entity/LivingEntity split.
- THE TEST-SIDE DISCOVERIES the physics drove (all in the tests, the
  solver needed no repair after the first port): (1) the clip's own
  direction — the reference calls `collisionBox.intersectY(moverShape,
  limit)`, the collision box the receiver; (2) the grounded walker's
  convention — `LivingEntity.travel` runs the move BEFORE the gravity,
  so a standing body enters `move()` with the previous tick's small
  negative drift (-0.0784*0.98), and WITHOUT it `onGround` reads false
  on a flat walk (d4 = 0 never satisfies `d4 < 0.0`); (3) the stair
  climb takes TWO ticks at step height 0.5 (the first tick steps onto
  the base slab and clips at the tall back's near face — 12.5 - 0.3
  - 10.7 = 1.5 on the pin — the second clears the back), exactly the
  reference's own per-tick walk, NOT the one-tight smooth climb;

## Slice M4b-fix — the pre-move overlap lift

- **THE REGRESSION the protocol module caught**: the
  VehicleIntegrationTest's rail ride timed out waiting for the cart's
  teleports — the DIAG walk found the FIRECART test's plain cart
  SUNK to y=3.35 inside the dirt, directly under the rail test's new
  cart; the player's interact mounted the sunken body and the steers
  drove a buried cart.
- **THE ROOT CAUSE**: the engine's cart spawns place the CENTRE at
  the rail's ride offset (cellY + 0.06) or a fire test's flame cell
  — the box's feet 0.29 INTO the cell below, an overlap the
  reference never creates (vanilla spawns bodies clear of the
  ground) and the clip law cannot resolve (a box already inside
  another's span clips on neither axis — the Y clip requires the
  mover entirely above). The legacy landing had answered the same
  overlap with its snap-UP ({@code floor(feet) + 1.0 + half}); the
  solver's first port let the body sink forever.
- **THE FIX**: the pre-move overlap lift in
  `VehicleEntity.solverMove` — the boxes overlapping the body's
  CURRENT shape gathered before the move, the feet raised to the
  highest overlapped top (the same raise the legacy landing
  performed), then the solver move. A spawned-in-ground body stands
  where the legacy walk stood it — never sinks — and a properly
  resting body (feet exactly at a top, the half-open convention)
  lifts nothing.
- Evidence: the protocol module FULL 108 green (the rail ride again)
  + the vehicle/physics packages 81 green (full-suite-M4b-fix.log).

## Slice P6-lane — the first parallel gameplay execution lane

- **THE LANE**: the random-tick walk's compute-then-apply split — the
  in-range chunks group by their region, each region's pick
  COMPUTATION rides as one job on the `DomainWorkerPool` (pure,
  parallel), the applies run IN THE STABLE REGION ORDER on the tick
  lane (§6.2's one authoritative writer — the compute side never
  touches world state).
- **THE DERIVED STREAMS** (`RandomTickPicks`): per-(tick, region)
  deterministic — `streamFor(baseSeed, tick*P1, regionId*P2)` — so the
  sequential walk and the pool dispatch produce IDENTICAL picks by
  construction (the equivalence is a property of the stream, not a
  hope about scheduling).
- **THE TIME AXIS DISCOVERY**: the derivation reads the system's OWN
  `laneTick` counter, NOT `world.totalTicks()` — the direct-driven
  tests (RandomTickSystemTest's statistical guard loops) call `tick()`
  without the ticker, and a frozen time axis would freeze the derived
  stream with it: the same picks every call. The live wiring advances
  both counters together (one `tick()` per world tick).
- **THE OBSERVABILITY**: `parallelDispatchTicks()` — the count of
  walks that actually rode the pool; the test asserts it is > 0 armed
  and == 0 unarmed (never a silent sequential fallback).
- **THE GATE**: `torch.parallel-region-ticks` at boot (default OFF) +
  the multi-region gate `regions.size() > 1` (the whole-world default
  region size keeps every walk sequential until an operator configures
  a real split).
- **THE LOCKSTEP TEST DESIGN**: two identically-built worlds (same
  generator/seed, same light engine, same 2-chunk partition, same
  chunk generation order, same seeded apply randomness) driven
  tick-by-tick — one sequential, one on the pool — compared for EXACT
  state equality while BOTH differ from their initial snapshot. The
  earlier two-boot design could never work: two server boots can never
  align their absolute tick numbers, and the streams are per-tick.
- Evidence: `RandomTickLaneTest` 5 green (the lockstep equivalence,
  the live boot wiring through the real tick loop, the stream
  contract, the pick shape, the pool dispatch) +
  `RandomTickSystemTest` 3 green unchanged; the direct sweep
  block/world/concurrent **330 green**; the broad
  entity/physics/piston/scheduler/vehicle sweep green; the protocol
  module 108 (one documented load flake — DonkeyChest, green in
  isolation) (sweep-P6lane-*.log).

## Slice S1 — the world-delta save's compute-then-publish split (the FIRST serialization workload)

- **THE ADOPTION** (Phase 5's own contract shape): the save's two
  halves split along the §14 compute contract — the SERIALIZATION is
  the pure function (`WorldDeltaSerializer.serialize`: the immutable
  snapshot IN, the ZWD bytes OUT, no world read, no I/O) and it LEAVES
  THE TICK LANE (one job on the compute pool per save); the
  PUBLICATION (the temp write + the atomic move — the storage's own
  file half, `DeltaWorldStorage.writeSerialized`) rides the
  blocking-I/O lane — never a simulation worker; the snapshot build
  STAYS on the tick lane (the engine's own `snapshotDeltas` walk —
  §6.2's one authoritative writer, unchanged).
- **THE SEQUENCE GATE** (§15's "persistence must not publish an older
  snapshot over newer state"): every submission takes a monotonic
  sequence; inside the per-storage publication right a snapshot whose
  sequence is not the newest seen DROPS (its bytes discarded, never
  written); the dropped save's durability latch still releases — the
  newer content on disk satisfies the demand (the supersession rule).
- **THE WIRING**: `WorldSavePipeline` over the engine's own compute
  subsystem + I/O lane + simulation domain; `saveAllNow`'s delta saves
  (overworld/nether/end) ride it while the other stores keep their
  synchronous walks (S2+ adopts them); the caller waits for the
  snapshot build AND every publication latch (the 10s bounds
  preserved).
- **THE OBSERVABILITY** (the §22 measurement row):
  submitted/serialized/landed/staleDropped/serializeNanos — the
  off-tick engagement evidence and the before/after serialization
  measurement hook.
- Evidence: `WorldSavePipelineTest` 4/4 (the BYTE-IDENTITY equivalence
  — the pure serializer's bytes == the synchronous save's file, the
  round-trip load restores the same deltas; the live pipeline through
  the real lanes with the telemetry + the off-tick measurement; the
  §15 gate — the older sequence never lands, the newest sequence owns
  the file; the superseded save's latch releases) + the persistence
  restart sweep green (PersistenceAcceptance/PlayerDataPersistence/
  FurnaceRestart/ContainerPersistence/CommandStatsPersistence/
  StorageBoundary). Landed at 062bea6e; docs row landed with this
  commit (the Wave S ledger section + the Phase-5 TWO WORKLOADS
  status).

## Slice S2 — the container trio's compute-then-publish split (the SECOND serialization workload)

- **THE SPLIT** (the S1 shape's own second adoption): each store's save

  SHALLOW map copy whose values are the LIVE entities; the capture
  walks them into the `Slot`/`Row` records so the serializer never
  reads a live entity, §31.6's snapshot-before-I/O), the SERIALIZE (the
  pure function: the immutable snapshot IN, the ZFD/ZCD/ZHD bytes OUT,
  no world read, no I/O), and the PUBLICATION (the temp write + the
  atomic move — the file half, safe off the tick lane).
- **THE BYTE-IDENTITY**: the byte walk is the historical save walk's
  own — same magic/version, same rows, same slot encoding (the EMPTY
  stack in a real slot and the never-touched slot both encode byte 0),
  same map order — proven against the pre-S2 interleaved walk
  replicated as the reference in the test. The synchronous `save`
  composes `writeSerialized(serialize(capture(live)))` — one
  serializer, one file half, the sync bytes and the pipeline bytes
  identical by construction; zero call-site churn on the old walk.
- **THE NAMED PATH**: `WorldSavePipeline.submitSave(name, snapshot,
  serializer, publisher)` — the same two halves as the typed
  world-delta path under the NAMED sequence gate (`publishNamed`: the
  per-storage lock + the monotonic per-name landed sequence, the named
  storages gate independently); `saveAllNow`'s trio saves ride it when
  booted — the deep capture stays on the tick lane inside the save
  walk, the serialization and the file half leave it, the caller waits
  for the trio's publication latches with the delta saves' (the 10s
  bounds preserved); the un-pipelined fallback keeps the sync form.
- **THE RELEASE-ON-FAILURE ARM** (both paths): a publication that
  fails loudly releases the save's durability latch before the failure
  rethrows to the lane (the lane logs SEVERE + counts the failure; the
  caller's walk never hangs on the failed save — the old walk's
  loud-failure contract with the async latch shape).

## The pathfinding offload gate — answered with measurements (374216f)

- **THE CONTRACT**: `PathRegion` — the pathfinding workload's explicit
  input (§6.5): the reachable box's material grid (one flat byte array,
  the CellMaterial ordinals), captured on the owning lane. The box
  bounds proven sound analytically (the g-cost cap bounds every
  reachable node within 2r per axis; the capture takes 2r + 2 with the
  body/scan margin) AND empirically (the node-for-node equivalence,
  including the closest-node fallback that explores the whole reachable
  set).
- **THE EQUIVALENCE** (PathRegionContractTest): the snapshot search and
  the live search agree node-for-node at both engine follow ranges —
  the reachable route, the wall-detour fallback (the wall placed inside
  the range band: the vanilla neighbor gate only proposes nodes within
  range of the target), and the beyond-range refusal.
- **THE MEASUREMENTS** (the §22 gate's bar): range 8 — live 12.4µs,
  capture 294µs, snapshot 7.2µs (34,656 cells); range 16 — live 18.7µs,
  capture 1,363µs, snapshot 8.8µs (196,000 cells).
- **THE VERDICT**: the eager capture costs 24-73x the on-lane search —
  the offload is a MEASURED NET LOSS at the engine's AI shape (the
  staggered 20-30-tick re-paths produce no batch; the ranges are 8/16).
  REJECTED WITH EVIDENCE per the §7 discipline (task overhead is part
  of the design). THE REOPEN CONDITIONS: the section-palette capture
  (~1000x fewer mappings), a batch AI shape sharing one region cache,
  or ranges far beyond 16.
- Evidence: PathRegionContractTest 3/3 + the pathing package 22/0.

## The GenLayer layout (VIII14's second slice, 2026-10-21)

The coordinator's lane on feature/biome-genlayer — the ~30-layer
transformation stack whole (the reference's world/biome/layer package,
21 classes ported verbatim) and the generator wired to it.

**The stack** — Layer's LCG scrambling (the 6364136223846793005 /
1442695040888963407 pair, three flavors: ctor salt, world-seed mix,
chunk-seed walk) + the init chain: Island (the 1-in-10 land roll with
the origin pin), FuzzyZoom, the AddIsland ladder, RemoveTooMuchOcean,
AddSnow (the 1/3/4 temperature bands), the three AddEdge modes (the
COOL_WARM blend, the HEAT_ICE lift, the SPECIAL 4-bit marker that
dispatches the mesa pair / jungle / mega taiga), the zooms,
MushroomIsland (the 1-in-100 isle), DeepOcean (the cross census),
RiverInit (the 299999 markers), BiomeInit (the four tables), BiomeEdge
(the hills' temperature validity, the mesa/mega-taiga strict edges, the
desert-against-ice EXTREME_HILLS+, the swamp's flips), RegionHills (the
hills table + the +128 mutation band + the 3-neighbor census), River
(the parity curve), Smooth, the sunflower 1-in-57, Shore (the five
shore laws), OceanRiverMixer (the river draw), VoronoiZoom (the ±1.8
corner jitter — the block-level grain).

**The wiring** — biomeAt answers the block-level voronoi map (the
chunk-aligned bounded cache, the reference's BiomeCache shape);
heightAt couples to the 1:4 grid biome's registration height pair (the
NAMED ADAPTATION: the engine's fbm stands in for the reference's
4-noise density stack — the land/ocean coherence the law, the
block/grid boundary warp the vanilla shore fuzz itself); the surface
materials consult the registration table's surfaceLegacyId (the sand
family skin, the stone beach, the mycelium isle, the spikes' snow, the
mesa's red sand); the spawn scan rides the reference's 7-row allowlist
(BiomeSource.biomesForSpawnPoint).

**The slice's own catch** — the reference's IntCache two-band pool
LEAKS the small band (tcache feeds only from the large band's
discards, and the large pool is always drained by the next query's own
pushes before pop ever sees it): harmless at the reference's query
volume (the BiomeCache's 30-second hit window serves most reads) but
fatal at the engine's per-chunk sampling (the sweep's 16k queries leak
~200k arrays and OOM the worker — found by the standalone probe after
the executor died wordlessly twice). The engine's unified size-aware
pool recycles every array: 245 total allocations across the whole
16k-query sweep. The adaptation is named in the javadoc with the full
why.

**The find on the way** — the voronoi boundary warp: the block biome
and the terrain height derive from the same 1:4 grid but the jitter
warps the block answers across cell boundaries (~20% of ocean-answering
blocks sit dry at cell edges; the river band's wet core is ~21% of its
block extent) — the vanilla shape itself (vanilla's rivers famously
read dashed at block level), pinned with the coherence tests' majority
bands rather than false absolutes.

Evidence: GenLayerLayoutTest 8 (the island pin, every temperature
family + ocean + rivers + mutated forms generating, the coherence, the
deep-ocean depth, the height bands, the voronoi grain, the per-seed
determinism, the surface skins) + the worldgen suites 77/0 + the
world/spawn/entity 632/0 + the block families 462/0 + the named
packages 385/0 + the root classes 399 (one documented await-flake,
isolated-green) + protocol 117 (one donkey await-flake, isolated-green)
+ bukkit 38/0 + launcher 47/0 + api 19/0 + the standalone distribution
probe (plains 1841 / forest 2988 / desert 53 / ocean 1447 / other 10055
over a 2048² sweep — the whole table generating).

### The additive families (VIII13's own ledger rows)

`MovingBlockEntity.moveEntities` lines 80-115's law is uniform —
`world.getEntities(null, box)` pushes EVERY body family, none exempted
— so the seam's five remaining families each gain their own box test,
shift arm, and fling arm, registered in the EngineServer push-surface
walk beside the three landed adapters:

- **The XP orbs**: `ExperienceOrbEntity.pushBy` — the item family's
  own leading-face clamped shift over the orb's Ground (the family's
  own unify note — the orb reuses the item model), the manager's
  `pushOrb` publishing the move through the orb's own listener face
  (the observers see the pushed orb the same tick, never waiting for
  the next physics pass to notice the displacement), the fling the
  public `setVelocity` composition.
- **The armor stands**: `ArmorStandSystem.pushStand` over the family's
  OWN walk law (the two-cell horizontal clip — the feet cell and the
  head cell above it — and the descending floor clip; the ascending
  axis unclipped, the family's walk carrying no ceiling arm, named),
  the marker stand never a body (updateSize(0, 0)), the new `small()`
  flag row with the per-form box (0.5 × 1.975 vs 0.25 × 0.9875), the
  fling the walk's own `setVelocity` (the friction decay carrying it).
- **The primed TNT**: `TntSystem.pushTnt` — the horizontal axes
  integrate unclipped (the family's established plain-integration
  shape, named), the descending axis clamped by the tick's own
  feet-relative consult, the fling the per-axis velocity set over the
  private fields.
- **The falling blocks**: `FallingBlockEntity.pushBy` — the tick's
  own two-path discipline (the `EntityMoveSolver` swept box over the
  ground's collision world when it provides the surface, the plain
  point consults otherwise, the descending clamp at the support's
  exact top), the manager's `pushFalling` publishing `onFallingMoved`,
  the fling VERTICAL-only (the family's flight integrates velocityY
  alone — the horizontal components have no carrier, named).
- **The projectiles**: `ProjectileManager.pushProjectile` — the
  leading-face clamped shift over the manager's SolidQuery with the
  per-kind box (the reference's own setSize rows: the arrow 0.5,
  the fireball base 1.0, the small fireball and the wither skull
  0.3125, the thrown family 0.25), the move published through the
  family's listener face. THE GROUNDED ARROW rides the same law as
  the reference's own outcome: `world.getEntities` displaces it and
  `ProjectileEntity.tick` lines 84-92's revalidation reads the STICK
  CELL, which the push never changes — the displaced arrow keeps its
  stick (the engine's grounded model carries the same shape), and
  the fling's set components ride as dead state exactly as the
  reference's stick branch leaves them.

The wiring: the walk gains the five families' box tests (the orb's
0.25 center box, the stand's per-form box rows, the TNT and the
falling block's 0.98 bottom-center box, the projectile's per-kind
half) + the five adapter records
(PistonOrbPush/PistonStandPush/PistonTntPush/PistonFallingPush/
PistonProjectilePush) beside the landed three.

### The retract-event resolver (the bukkit slice-2 wave's recorded bug)

The native PistonMoveEvent's javadoc names "the pull chain on a
sticky retract" as the movedCells intent, but the gate's fresh
resolution walked the pull column from the block beyond the head
toward the piston and hit the EXTENDED HEAD itself — a
BEHAVIOR_BLOCK cell, the reference's own material table — so every
sticky retract answered movedCells=[] while the pull itself landed
(the bukkit test pinned the actual shape with the comment naming the
follow-up). The fix mirrors the movement's own pre-steps in the
gate's prospective resolution: (1) the retract arm removes the head
BEFORE its resolver runs (PistonBaseBlock.move lines 288-290), so
`PistonStructureResolver` gains the prospective form — a
`departedCell` that answers AIR through the whole walk (every getBlock
read routed through the new `blockAt` helper); (2) the arm's own pull
gate (doEvent lines 141-143, verbatim) — a DESTROY block (the old
gate even answered brokenCells rows the arm never breaks), an
immovable one, or a mid-flight carrier leaves the lists empty exactly
as the movement leaves the world alone; (3) the plain retract answers
the empty lists the event javadoc itself names (nothing follows the
head home).

### The Phase-7 merge bucketing's landing record

The optimization itself landed at d100b55 (the O(n^2) candidate scan
retired; the equivalence pinned per-seed by
ItemMergeBucketingEquivalenceTest 12 against a verbatim copy of the
old law), but the §22 Phase-7 row still named it as the pending
demand-named fix. This slice records the landing with fresh
re-measured numbers on this machine (the DenseOwnerProfilingTest
harness's own methodology): 458 settled items → itemEntities
1671.7us/tick (3.65us/item) against the pre-bucketing 2726.4us at 444
(6.14us/item); 1532 settled → 5482.0us/tick (3.58us/item) against the
pre-bucketing 16127.3us at 1506 (10.71us/item, 91.3% of the tick fan)
— the relief at the recorded ~1500-item density is 2.94x and the
per-item growth is 0.98x for 3.34x the bodies (the pre-bucketing
superlinear signature was 1.74x): the superlinear term is retired.

Task ID: rcon-listener-race-hotfix
Agent: the coordinator (Abasing session)
Task: Run #375's red suite diagnosed and fixed — the RconBase.start()
flag/thread race (the silently-dead-listener shape), found by the
release pipeline's own evidence.

Work Log:
- The trigger: the PR #38 merge's confirming run (#375, the first
  COMPLETED suite run on the final wave-3 state — #373/#374 were
  cancelled by the successive pushes) failed at the suite step on both
  attempts: attempt 1 the four RconEngineRouteIntegrationTest
  ConnectExceptions + QueryResponseHandlerTest.theWrongChallengeIsIgnored
  (line 101); attempt 2 (the retry) QueryResponseHandlerTest
  .theHandshakeTokenLaw (the SAME line 101, a different method).
- The diagnosis trail: the RCON class's bootEngine asserts HAD passed
  (both listeners non-null AND isRunning true) before every connect was
  refused — so the listener was born, then died, with the flag still
  true; the Query failures were the same shape on UDP (the handshake
  datagram answered by nothing). One root cause explains all five+one:
  RconBase.start() starts the worker thread BEFORE writing the running
  flag — the reference's own order (RconBase line 16) — and the JMM
  gives the worker no guarantee it will observe the write: on the
  loaded 2-core CI runner the scheduler can run the listener thread
  first, the `while (running)` condition reads false, the loop exits
  into its own finally (closing the freshly bound listener), and the
  parent's write lands afterward — isRunning() true, socket closed.
  TCP answers ConnectException; UDP answers silence (the 2s timeout
  surfaces as the line-101 "the handshake always replies" failure).
  Each QueryResponseHandlerTest method rolls a fresh handler = a fresh
  roll of the dice; the engine boot rolls once per class.
- The fix (one reorder, RconBase.start): the flag flips BEFORE
  Thread.start() — the happens-before edge of start() makes the loop's
  first read a guaranteed-visible true; a stop() landing between the
  write and the start still ends correct (the loop reads false, exits,
  the finally closes the listener like a stopped server). Covers all
  three RconBase children (RconServer accept, QueryResponseHandler
  receive, RconClient session). The javadoc names the race, the JMM
  reasoning, and the run #375 evidence; §32.4 records it as the SECOND
  named start() difference (the reference could live with the shape —
  process-exit lifecycle; a long-running engine server cannot).
- The test hardenings (the #361-family pattern — harden the assert to
  the condition it needs): RconEngineRouteIntegrationTest.bootEngine's
  two asserts now demand the live thread beside the flag (in-package
  protected access; the fields are assigned only after start() returns,
  so no NPE window); QueryResponseHandlerTest.startHandler asserts the
  seat the same way, and theInvalidPortRefusalLawNeverBinds builds its
  handler inline (the refusal arm never starts a thread — the happy-path
  liveness law must not ride it). A future silent death now fails at
  boot, loudly, naming the shape — not as refused connects or a
  confusing line-101 timeout.
- NOT changed: the ephemeral-port probe pattern (bind-then-release) —
  the port-steal theory explains only the Query symptom and fails the
  RCON one (a stolen port fails bootEngine's assert loudly, never the
  refused-connect shape); the flag race explains every observed failure
  with one cause. No ML-002 census follow-up — this is a start-ordering
  race, not a deadline family.

Stage Summary:
- The engine's remote-admin listeners can no longer silently die at
  boot on a loaded machine; the pipeline's confirming run for the PR
  #38 merge rides the fix push (the next release stamps 131).

Task ID: TF-5
Agent: Abasing (the coding session)
Task: The CI-caught regression repair — the join-flow family's failure on the pre-session HEAD (f3221566), traced and fixed.

Work Log:
- The CI run on f3221566 (and f7af2ad2 before it) failed on
  JoinFlowIntegrationTest (statusPing twice, the outdated/duplicate/
  invalid arms with broken pipes); the failures are deterministic in
  isolation locally (3 of 7).
- The bisect by CI history: the last green run 37d5ef7c, the first
  failure f7af2ad2 — the ML-008 commit (the /give alignment, whose
  scripted-client changes added the keep-alive auto-answer).
- The root cause: the keep-alive packet id (0x00) collides with the
  STATUS response and the LOGIN disconnect on the wire — the
  auto-answer answered those as keep-alives, writing an invalid packet
  into the pre-play states and the server's default arm closed the
  channel (the status ping's lost pong, the login arms' broken pipes).
- The fix: the client's own inPlayState flag, set at readLoginSuccess
  (the state switch where 0x00 becomes the keep-alive alone) — the
  auto-answer runs in PLAY alone; the 120 login call sites all route
  through readLoginSuccess, the raw-frame conformance tests never
  needed the answering, and the timeout test's silence arm keeps its
  opt-out.
- JoinFlowIntegrationTest 7/7 green again; the full protocol suite
  verified after the fix.

Stage Summary:
- The ML-008 scripted-client regression repaired (fc91e59c): the
  lesson — the scripted client's wire-level conveniences must be
  state-aware, because the 1.8 protocol's packet ids collide across
  states (0x00 is the status response, the login disconnect, AND the
  keep-alive, one per state).

squared-distance range, every sendMob* send gated on the mob's
dimension, the fans gated where the body is at hand.

**The completion session (this entry):** (1) the handoff's core

63/0; (2) the open verifications closed — the protocol module whole
203/0 over every suite class (batched for the runner's ten-minute
wall: 76/0 light, 41/0 medium, 57/0 heavy integration, 27/0
acceptance, WorldgenDeterminismRunTest, AttributionLoadTest at 80s),

tails ALL CLOSED; the armor-stand/fireworks/ender-eye families stay
honest overworld-0 emitters until their own slices demand the carry),

**Evidence:** FxDimensionReadsTest 3/0 + FishingSystemTest's

**Lessons:** (1) the scheduled batches can collide — two instances
of the same 3-hour timer landed the same lane within the same window;
the pushed handoff wins over the local duplicate, and the resolution
is the repository-safety law (never force-push, preserve the pushed
work, ledger the decision); (2) a handoff commit with an explicit
open-verifications list is the cheapest possible recovery shape —
the next instance's first task was named in the commit message
itself, and the verification batches finished in one session.

## 2026-10-28 — the §35 transport lane closed whole (Waves T-2 ledgered, T-3 the pooled-allocation adoption, T-4 the wedged-loop ceiling; the release pipeline repaired twice over)

**The pipeline repair first (6c73933d):** run 1070ecff failed twice —
the fat jar could not expand zamin-transport's jar ("does not exist"),
and ComputeSubsystemTest's recovery arm tripped on the loaded runner.
Root causes: (1) fatServerJar's explicit jar edges never gained the
transport row when Wave T-1 brought the module into the runtime
classpath (the eager .files resolution carries no task dependencies —
the exact reason api/core/protocol are listed); (2) the test pinned a
queued-depth SNAPSHOT the idle worker can steal between submit and
assert. Fixed: the build edge + the recovery arm re-pinned on the
after-job's completion latch (the admission reopening is the submit's
acceptance, never the snapshot); the fat-jar failure reproduced from
the clean-jar state and verified green, the test 3/3 stable. The
owner's §35 marker comment retired with the same commit (the section
stands in its numeric position; the owner note already withdrawn).

**Wave T-2 ledgered (0fe24c4e):** slices A+B (the latency ring, the
benchmark matrix, the urgent-lane coalescing repair, the leak
detector at advanced/paranoid) had landed as code without their §29
rows — the rows landed with the pipeline repair recorded inside them.

**Wave T-3 — the §35.4 pooled-allocation adoption:** the harness
(PacketAllocationBenchmarkTest) runs §35.4's compare list over the
engine's own encode shapes under three arms (heap-unpooled /
pooled-heap / pooled-direct) at three sizes, with the byte-identity
admission row (every arm produces identical bytes — the encode law is
allocator-independent). The numbers split by SHAPE: at 16 KiB pooled
wins 5-10x (685K-1.29M pps vs 126K; ~120 B/packet thread-alloc vs
16,448 — the whole frame became young-gen garbage per packet, the
attribution pass's #1 byte[] finding; zero collections vs a 12 ms
one); at 24-192 B heap-unpooled wins 2-7x (11.7M vs 1.6M pps small —
the TLAB bump beats the arena path) and pooled would only add its
4 MiB retained arenas. The adoption follows the numbers exactly: the
three chunk-window frame sites (the 0x21 single, the 0x21 partial,
the 0x26 bulk — the engine's only large outbound allocations) now ask
POOLED.directBuffer behind a named constant carrying the measured
numbers in its javadoc; the 190 small sites keep Unpooled.buffer
(their measured win); the serializer's byte[] intermediates stay heap
honestly (the 1:1-pinned walk, its own future slice). The pipeline
was verified direct-compatible FIRST (zero .array()/hasArray() on any
outbound path — the one .array() site is the inbound decrypt
decoder's own heap ask).

**Wave T-4 — the §35.13 wedged-loop ceiling (the §35.11 kill-policy
row closed as the fail-safely law):** the domain split the evidence
dictates — a slow SOCKET never grows the engine queue (the drain
still writes; Netty's own ChannelOutboundBuffer absorbs the
backpressure exactly as the reference's per-packet writeAndFlush
shape did — vanilla never kicks a slow socket), only a STOPPED event
loop does (the wedged benchmark shape: the 1 MiB observable crossed
at enqueue #1024, the caller never blocked, 0 writes). The ceiling:
past 64 MiB queued (64x the observable; the healthy face answers 20
packets/flush at a 6us dwell, so 64 MiB is a loop SECONDS behind — a
dead loop, not a slow one) the crossing enqueue releases its own
ticket (counted, never silent), the connection closes NOW (every
queued ticket released, nothing leaks), the severe warning names the
channel, and the new wedgedCloses row lands in the metrics snapshot;
never throws — the simulation lanes must not see gameplay exceptions
from a transport protection.

**Evidence:** the allocation harness 2/0 with every arm's numbers
printed for the ledger; OutboundQueueTest's new ceiling pin (63 MiB
absorbs alive, the 64th MiB closes with every ticket released under
the paranoid detector, one wedgedCloses row, admission shut after);
transport 21/0; the protocol module over ALL 71 classes green in
eight batches (the environment reaps detached gradle processes — the
batched-with-timeout shape is the runner's law); bukkit + launcher
green, the packaged console verified on torch-1.8.8-151.

**Lessons:** (1) a new module in the runtime classpath needs its fat-
jar edge the same day it gains a project dependency — the eager
.configurations resolution silently hides the missing task dependency
until a clean runner schedules the merge before the jar exists;
(2) a queued-depth snapshot after a submit is a race with the worker
that serves the queue — pin completions, never snapshots; (3) the
pooled decision is per-SHAPE, not per-engine — the small-packet storm
is the TLAB's home turf, the chunk windows are the arena's, and the
adoption split along the measured line; (4) the kill policy's real
domain is the WEDGED loop, not the slow socket — naming the domain
correctly closed the row without inventing a gameplay policy the
reference never had.

## 2026-10-28 — the silk & shears parity audit (PR #57, the second verifier pass after the tall-grass fix)

The verifier role, second pass: the drop-band audit (PR #56) fixed the
count bands; this pass swept the OTHER half of the same law family —
the silk-touch and shears gates — and found seventeen gaps in one
read. The reference law that anchored the whole sweep: the default
silk gate is `hasSilkTouchDrops() = isCube() && !hasBlockEntity`
(Block.java lines 784-787) — every full cube silk-harvests ITSELF
unless the class overrides — and the shears laws ride
afterMinedByPlayer's own arm. The pre-fix engine carried a
hand-curated silk set (SILK_TOUCHABLE) that missed every cube whose
by-hand row diverges from the block.

The finds, in reach order: the glowstone band answered dust under silk
(the audit's own "ALWAYS" claim in PR #56 missed the silk arm — the
verifier's first catch was against the previous verifier's own
commit); the melon's slice walk ignored silk; the LIT redstone ore's
empty-stack quirk (Item.byBlock of the lit form resolves null — the
dig-start light swap means the lit form is the one actually broken, so
silk on redstone ore answers NOTHING in the reference); the mining-XP
hook fired under silk (the silk arm replaces the whole drop walk —
the XP carrier never runs); the lit form had no XP row at all, so
redstone ore paid NO XP (the unlit row was unreachable through the
same swap); the vine had no shears branch; the double plant's lower
shears arm was missing entirely and the upper pair arm answered ONE
tallgrass where the reference drops TWO (line 189's ItemStack count);
the glass pane and all thirty-two stained glass blocks had no silk
arm (the stained pair need the COLOR in the damage field — the
generic silk arm cannot express a damage domain, so a dedicated
branch owns them); the cobweb had no drop row AT ALL (every break
answered nothing); the podzol and coarse dirt had no rows either
(the podzol's hand/silk split rides the dirt item's damage domain);
and the quartz ore, clay, snow block and mycelium all answered their
by-hand rows under silk.

Two registrations fell out of the sweep: the vine/cobweb/glass
pane/quartz ore items (declared nowhere, wire ids already mapped —
LegacyBlockIds carried 106/30/102/153 all along), and the glowstone
BLOCK item itself — declared for the cleric's trade stock but never
in the registration list, the same declared-but-never-registered
shape the Slice 65 comment warns about, found by the audit's first
test run when the new silk gate's lookup threw.

**Evidence:** SilkAndShearsParityAcceptanceTest 10/0; the block
package whole 243/0 (the DropBandParity + TallGrass + DoublePlant +
Melon + Mineral + Farming seats included); interaction + experience
24/0; MiningXpAcceptanceTest + Silverfish + RegistryApi +
DyeFamilyPlacement green; the protocol module's ItemRegistryParity +
LegacyBlockIdsIntegrity + BlockRegistryTest green over the four new
registrations.

**Lessons:** (1) an audit's own claims need the same verification as
the code it audits — the glowstone band was pinned "ALWAYS" against
every tool while the reference's silk arm sat three lines above the
walk the band came from; (2) the empty-stack quirk class (lit
redstone ore has NO registered item, so silk drops nothing) is real
vanilla law, not an edge to smooth over — the dig-start light swap
makes the unreachable-looking form the ONLY reachable one, and the
lit XP row's absence meant the ore paid no XP AT ALL in practice;
(3) the declared-but-never-registered item shape keeps resurfacing —
every new item-consuming gate (silk lookups, creative claims, trade
stock) should sweep the list against the declared constants.

## 2026-10-28 — the smelting-completion parity audit (PR #58, the verifier's third pass)

The third sweep, one family over: the smelting tables. The reference's
SmeltingManager keys BOTH sides of the law on the result STACK — the
recipe by input item AND metadata, the take XP by output item AND
metadata (lines 25-64). The engine's tables keyed the plain identifiers
alone, so every row whose input or output rode the damage field never
landed: the rabbit had NO smelting row at all (the item registered with
its own smelt comment back in Slice 11i — the row never landed, the
same declared-but-never-carried shape the silk audit caught twice), the
cactus's green dye, the default stone brick's cracked form, the wet
sponge's dried form — and the coal pair's take split: the ore take
pays 0.1 and the charcoal take 0.15 over the SAME item id, so the
pre-fix identifier-keyed table paid the charcoal's band for every coal
ore take.

The fix followed the reference's own keying: two plain rows (rabbit,
cactus→dye:2), two damage-aware resultOf gates (stone bricks damage 0
alone → cracked; sponge damage 1 alone → dried — the furnace entity
already consulted resultOf(type, damage) for the fish family, so the
rows flow unchanged), and a damage-keyed take law beside the identifier
table. The take path in EngineServer now passes the taken stack's
damage exactly like the reference's getXp consult.

**Evidence:** SmeltingCompletionParityTest 6/0 (the rabbit's smelt and
take, the cactus's green dye with the no-other-dye-pays pins, the stone
brick's plain-only gate with the mossy/chiseled exclusions, the wet
sponge's damage-1 gate, the coal pair's 0.1/0.15 split, the cactus's
end-to-end entity walk); MetadataSmeltingTest + FurnaceTakeXpAcceptanceTest
green unchanged (the fractional take split untouched); the furnace
package whole 35/0.

**Lessons:** (1) the damage field is a second key axis everywhere an
identifier-keyed table answers — the coal split hid in plain sight
because BOTH smelts were already implemented and green-tested; the law
was right for one and wrong for the other; (2) the take XP can never
key the item id alone when the id hosts a damage domain (the dye item
answers ink sac AND the cactus's green — only the green is a smelting
result); (3) the registered-with-a-comment pattern is the declared-but-
never-carried shape's signature — the rabbit's own registration comment
NAMED the smelt the table never carried.

## 2026-10-28 — the tool-wear parity audit (PR #59, the verifier's fourth pass)

The fourth sweep, one family over: the durability wear. The anchor law
lives in the item classes, not the block path — ToolItem.mineBlock wears
ONE (line 42), SwordItem.mineBlock TWO (line 55), ToolItem.attack TWO
(line 35), SwordItem.attack ONE (line 48), ShearsItem.mineBlock ONE on
its own six-member band alone (lines 20-29), and the shears and hoes
extend Item directly so their attack arm NEVER wears. The engine had
folded all of it into one flat wear-one-everywhere row — and broke the
stack at damage >= maxDurability where the reference's takeDamage
breaks at metadata > maxDamage (line 204).

The boundary was the silent find: the >= shape cost every damageable
item exactly ONE use (an iron pickaxe answered 250 where the reference
answers 251, a gold pickaxe 32 where it answers 33), every wear site
carried it (damageHeld, wearArmor, wearArmorStack, the mob thorns
walk), and FOUR existing tests had pinned it — the gold-pickaxe seat,
the armor helmet seat, the thorns frail-helmet seat, the survival
tool-break dig — each re-pinned to the reference's own count. The
zombie's sun-helmet walk was verified BEFORE touching it: the
reference's own setDamage walk (ZombieEntity lines 165-172) carries its
own >= boundary, the one place the flat shape was already 1:1 — left
alone with a note.

The wear split landed as two shared rows (Tools.blockWearOf /
meleeWearOf) and one block band (BlockBehaviorTable.inShearsWearBand),
so the dig site, the two melee sites and the tests read one table; the
shears band keeps the dead bush and the double plants OUTSIDE exactly
(the reference registers the band by block, never by flora — the
contrast the tall-grass slice's own shears law needed spelled out).

**Evidence:** ToolWearParityTest 5/0 (the survive-at-max law over both
edges, the 251-use full walk, the two wear tables, the band's six
members and four exclusions); the four re-pinned seats green;
PlayerInventoryTest + ToolsTest + ArmorTest + SurvivalMining +
ThornsMobVictim + SilkAndShears + DropBandParity + BlockBehaviorTable
green; the block + interaction packages and the combat seats 274/0.

**Lessons:** (1) a boundary constant is a law — one character of >=
vs > silently cost every damageable item in the engine one use, and
four green tests had pinned the wrong answer as "exactly as
historically"; (2) the re-pin test is the verifier's sharpest tool:
when a test's assertion contradicts the reference source, the
reference wins and the seat gets re-pinned with the law named in its
message; (3) one law, one shape — the zombie's own setDamage walk
carrying its own boundary is the counterexample that proves the wear
family is not one law but several, and each was read before it was
touched.

## 2026-10-28 — the mining-speed parity audit (PR #60, the verifier's fifth pass)

The fifth sweep, one family over: the mining-speed law — the five
per-item getMiningSpeed overrides, the canMineBlock gate the /30-vs-/100
divisor rides, and the two status-effect multipliers the five-arg
MiningRules shape's own javadoc had promised "once the engine grows a
status-effect system" (the system — potions, the beacon's haste, the
elder-guardian fatigue aura — had since grown without the multipliers
landing).

The speed table had folded all five item classes into one material-string
class match paying the tool's tier on a match alone. What that lost: the
SWORD's whole law (15.0 on the web block identity, 1.5 on the
PLANT/REPLACEABLE_PLANT/CORAL/LEAVES/PUMPKIN band — the table answered
1.0 everywhere, a diamond sword never out-digging a fist on its own web);
the SHEARS' own band (15.0 web and leaves, 5.0 wool — the class match
paid the shears' IRON 6.0 on leaves and wool both, and the web row's null
material answered 1.0); the PICKAXE's effective-blocks set beyond its
material branch (the ICE and the RAIL pair — "rock" alone answered 1.0 on
all three); and the AXE's plant material branch (an iron axe digs tall
grass at the FULL 6.0 tier in the reference — the engine's "plants"
string sat outside every class map, so the whole flora answered 1.0, and
the map's own "plant" arm was dead code against the rows' "plants"
spelling).

The gate was the same fold: the reference's COBWEB material requires the
tool and the web's own breakers are the SWORD and the SHEARS together —
a two-class gate the single-class match could not answer, and the pre-fix
row was tool-free besides, so a bare hand took the string at the /30
divisor. The SNOW material requires the SHOVEL alone (the pre-fix rows
left both snow shapes hand-harvestable — a bare hand pocketed the snow
block's four snowballs, and the snow layer's own LAYERS+1 player arm
(afterMinedByPlayer lines 102-106) was missing ENTIRELY, the Slice 17d
comment having folded the player arm into the generic arm's empty walk
— the misread this pass re-pinned at the row AND at the gated walk, so
the player dig answers 2 while the generic arm the wash-out feeds keeps
the reference's own zero). PACKED_ICE requires NO tool (Material line 27
— the row's requires-tool had every non-pickaxe hand digging at /100
where the reference answers /30). And the material strings the speed
table exposed went honest one row at a time: the CACTUS is its own
material (out of both the axe branch and the sword band), the PUMPKIN
trio is Material.PUMPKIN (the sword's 1.5 band member, the axe's set
member), the BOOKSHELF is WOOD (the null material had the axe at 1.0),
the skull family is DECORATION, and the flower pots' slice comment said
DECORATION while its string said "plant".

The haste/fatigue multipliers landed in MiningRules' own order (between
the Efficiency add and the environment divisors, the reference's lines
663-695) over a new effect-amplifier hook the server wires to the potion
system. The fourth pass's own boundary law found one missed seat in the
net: UnbreakingAcceptanceTest's breaking-piece seat had stayed pinned to
the pre-fix >= boundary in the enchantment package the fourth pass's
sweep never listed — re-pinned with the law named (the piece survives AT
its maximum, the exceed breaks it).

**Evidence:** MiningSpeedParityTest 11/0 (the sword's 15/1.5 rows, the
shears' 15/5/1 band, the pickaxe's effective set, the axe's plant branch
and set, the shovel family whole, the hoe's never, the web's two-class
gate with the 8-tick/400-tick divisor split, the snow pair's shovel gate
with the 10-tick/1-tick layer split and the wash-out's generic zero, the
packed-ice 15-tick hand dig, the haste/fatigue multipliers in the
reference's own order, the plant family's four-class split with the
shears' wear band kept beside its 1.0 speed); the re-pinned seats green
(DropBand's shovel-snow seat, SilkAndShears' silk-shovel snow and
sword-web seats, Unbreaking's boundary seat); the block package whole
254/0; item + interaction + potion 49/0; enchantment 58/0; the timing and
family batch 75/0 (VanillaMiningTiming, SurvivalMining, DigHandlerGates,
MiningXp, BlockInteraction, Melon, CaneAndCactus, DyeFamily,
GroundCover, RailBlocks, MapColors, StepSound); the combat and player
batch 109/0.

**Lessons:** (1) the speed family is five laws over one table, not one
class-match — the reference answers per ITEM class (the sword and the
shears both carry their own full rows, and the axe's material branch
covers blocks its effective set never named); (2) the same flag gates
three walks — the divisor, the drops, and the wear's hardness gate all
consult canMineBlock, so a wrong requiresTool is never just a timing
bug (the bare hand was TAKING the string and the snowballs); (3) a
player-only drop law cannot ride the drop ROW — the reference's own
split (getBaseDropCount 0 + afterMinedByPlayer layers+1) needs the
player arm at the gated walk or the wash-out pays it too; (4) a promised
law's javadoc is a ledger — "once the engine grows a status-effect
system" was written by an author who did not know the system had already
grown; the verifier reads the promise AND the ground.
